Newborn Care

Flat head syndrome in babies: plagiocephaly and safe sleep

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A baby’s skull is flexible so the brain can grow. Repeated pressure on one area can produce a flat spot, called positional or deformational plagiocephaly when it affects one side. Many cases improve with growth and movement. An unusual head shape should still be assessed, and preventing flattening must never replace safe sleep.

Positional flattening is different from fused skull sutures

Positional plagiocephaly usually flattens one side at the back of the head; the ear and forehead on that side may shift forward, creating a parallelogram appearance from above. Brachycephaly is a more even flattening across the back with a wider head. The joints between skull bones remain open.

Craniosynostosis is a different, uncommon condition in which one or more skull sutures fuse too early. It may be present from birth, but a positional flattening can also begin before birth; “congenital plagiocephaly” is not a reliable synonym for craniosynostosis. Some cases are isolated and others are associated with genetic syndromes such as Apert or Crouzon. Assessment distinguishes the causes.

What parents may notice

A flat area, uneven ears, forehead or facial asymmetry may become noticeable in the first weeks or months. A patch of rubbed hair can accompany pressure but does not diagnose the cause. Looking at the head from above, or when hair is wet, may make its shape easier to describe; appearance alone is not a home diagnostic test.

Tell the baby’s clinician about a hard ridge, worsening or unusual shape, persistent head tilt or difficulty turning the neck, or concerns about the soft spot or head growth. Fontanelles naturally vary in size and closure timing; a small or closed soft spot alone does not prove craniosynostosis. Do not press or manipulate the skull to test it.

Why positional flattening develops

The same area may receive repeated pressure when a baby strongly prefers looking one way or spends prolonged time lying down. Limited movement and little awake floor play can contribute. Prematurity, softer skull bones, extended hospital care, crowded conditions in multiple pregnancy and birth-related moulding, including assisted delivery, may be relevant. They do not prove a specific cause or mean a parent has failed.

Torticollis, or a tight neck muscle, can restrict turning and maintain a preference for one side. Other conditions affecting movement or vision can also lead to head tilt. Early assessment is useful rather than forcing the head around or assuming all tilting is muscular.

Keep sleep safe while varying awake positions

Place your baby on their back for every sleep, including naps, on a firm, flat, non-inclined sleep surface with a fitted sheet and an otherwise empty sleep space. Do not use side or tummy sleeping to correct flattening. Keep pillows, head-shaping cushions, wedges, positioners, loose blankets and toys out of the sleep space.

During awake time, vary carrying and feeding sides, hold the baby with their airway clear, and encourage comfortable turning toward your face or an interesting object. Limit unnecessary time in car seats, swings and bouncy seats; these can keep pressure on the head and are not a treatment for flat spots. Use the car seat correctly for travel and take the baby out when appropriate at the destination.

You can vary the baby’s orientation in the cot relative to the room to encourage looking toward different sights, while still placing them on their back. Keep the cot bare and do not secure the head in a chosen position. Repositioning advice should fit the baby’s neck movement and any other medical needs.

Tummy time is awake, closely supervised play

Offer tummy time only while the baby is awake and an attentive adult is closely watching. Use a safe floor play area, starting with brief comfortable sessions. If the baby becomes sleepy, move them to their safe sleep space on their back; the play mat is not a sleep surface.

AAP advice updated in September 2026 suggests starting with three to five minutes, two or three times daily, from coming home, gradually working toward a total of 15 to 30 minutes a day by seven weeks as tolerated. These are flexible starting goals, not a requirement to force a distressed baby or a universal 40-to-60-minute maximum. Premature or medically fragile babies may need an individualized plan.

Tummy play helps neck and shoulder strength and motor skills. Get down at the baby’s level, offer short enjoyable sessions, and ask for advice if turning or lifting the head is difficult. Vary awake floor play on the back as well; tummy time does not replace putting the baby on their back for sleep.

Assessment and when to ask for help

Ask for a clinical review when you notice flattening or have concerns about head shape, size or neck movement; early review leaves more time for appropriate management. The clinician checks head shape from different angles, head circumference and its growth pattern, sutures and fontanelles, neck movement, eyes, development and neurological findings.

Most positional flattening is diagnosed from history and examination without routine scans. If craniosynostosis is suspected, prompt referral to a craniofacial team is appropriate; that team selects imaging if needed. Do not delay referral to arrange your own CT, or assume every flat spot needs an X-ray.

A baby with a seizure, difficulty breathing, or who is very difficult to wake needs immediate emergency help. These are not ordinary symptoms of positional flattening. Report developmental, vision or hearing concerns rather than attributing them to head shape alone.

Physiotherapy and guided positioning

A paediatric physiotherapist can assess torticollis, head control and movement, teach safe handling and an individual exercise plan, and monitor improvement. Repositioning and physiotherapy are often the first steps for positional flattening; positioning pillows are not a safe substitute.

Do not stretch the neck forcefully or begin a routine copied from another child. Use only exercises demonstrated for your baby and ask about pain, resistance or lack of progress. Persistent severe flattening, worsening shape or torticollis that is not improving may need specialist review.

Helmet treatment: selected use and evidence limits

A custom cranial orthosis guides growth by allowing space over flatter areas. A specialist may consider it for persistent moderate-to-severe positional deformity after positioning or physiotherapy, or selected later presentations. Mild flattening does not automatically need a helmet, and a helmet alone does not treat fused sutures.

Recommendations differ. The 2016 CNS guideline supports selected helmet use with uncertain clinical certainty; RCH discusses selected severe cases, while January 2026 NHS advice says helmets are not provided for positional flat head because evidence of benefit is insufficient. Discuss severity, natural improvement, expected benefit, cost and alternatives with the local team.

Timing depends on growth, severity, corrected age for prematurity and response to other measures. AAP discusses possible benefit around five to six months when other measures have not helped; RCH commonly assesses suitability around six to seven months. There is no universal three-to-six-month rule or guaranteed correction in twelve weeks; benefit generally decreases as growth slows.

If prescribed, the helmet must be individually fitted and adjusted, with a wear and cleaning plan, often about 23 hours daily. Duration varies and may be several months. Skin irritation, persistent redness, discomfort or fit concerns need review by the fitting service; do not alter the helmet yourself. Perfect symmetry is not guaranteed.

Surgery belongs to a different assessment pathway

Surgery is not routine treatment for positional plagiocephaly. Craniosynostosis often needs specialist surgery to release or reshape affected skull bones and, in some cases, prevent pressure affecting the growing brain. Some mild cases are monitored; the decision depends on the suture, age and other findings.

A helmet may be used after selected craniosynostosis operations, but tummy time or an ordinary positional helmet cannot undo fused sutures. Some forms can involve vision, hearing or developmental problems and need ongoing multidisciplinary care. These complications are not inevitable, and surgery does not guarantee that every associated problem disappears.

Prevention, follow-up and outlook

You cannot prevent every difference in head shape. Safe awake position changes, supervised tummy play, alternating feeding or carrying sides and early help for restricted neck movement can reduce repeated pressure. Keep safe sleep consistent and do not blame yourself for a flat spot.

Positional flattening does not cause brain injury or developmental delay, although movement or developmental difficulties may coexist and should be assessed separately. Most head shapes improve as babies grow and become more mobile; some asymmetry can remain. Follow the agreed review plan, especially for severe or worsening changes, rather than assuming all cases will completely resolve.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

AAP September 2026 advice separates back-to-sleep from awake supervised tummy play and offers flexible starting goals.

NHS January 2026 and RCH advice support early assessment, safe awake positioning and physiotherapy for restricted neck movement.

CNS 2016 evidence-based guidance supports clinical diagnosis with selected imaging and physiotherapy rather than positioning pillows.

Helmet recommendations differ across CNS, AAP, RCH and NHS; selection and benefit should be discussed individually rather than promised.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to record head-shape changes, preferred turning side, awake play tolerance and questions for the baby’s clinician. Notes or photographs cannot diagnose fused sutures, measure skull pressure or replace head-growth and developmental assessment.

When to seek help

Keep every sleep on the back in a firm, flat, bare sleep space. Never use pillows, wedges or tummy sleeping to correct head shape. Tummy play needs an awake baby and close adult supervision. Seek prompt assessment for worsening shape, a ridge or limited neck movement, and emergency help for a seizure, breathing difficulty or extreme difficulty waking. Do not force neck stretches or buy a helmet without assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Positional flattening and craniosynostosis have different causes and need different assessment.
  • Always place babies on their backs for sleep in a firm, flat, bare sleep space; do not use head-shaping pillows.
  • Tummy time is for awake babies with close supervision, built up in short comfortable sessions.
  • Early neck-movement assessment and physiotherapy may help; helmets are selected, with differing recommendations and uncertain benefit.
  • Most positional flattening improves, but worsening shape, ridges, growth or developmental concerns need review.

Frequently asked questions

What causes a flat spot?

Repeated pressure on a flexible skull, a preferred head direction or limited neck movement can contribute. Prematurity and womb or birth moulding may also matter. Early fusion of sutures is a separate condition, not the explanation for every flat spot.

When should I ask for help?

Arrange a review for concerns about head shape, growth or neck turning, particularly worsening asymmetry, a hard ridge or persistent tilt. A clinician interprets the soft spot and growth together; do not diagnose from one sign. A seizure, breathing difficulty or extreme difficulty waking needs emergency help.

How can I reduce the chance of flattening?

Vary awake carrying and feeding sides, limit unnecessary time in seats, and provide supervised awake tummy play. Continue placing the baby on their back for every sleep in a bare, firm, flat sleep space. Never use pillows, wedges or prone sleep to change head shape.

Does positional plagiocephaly harm the brain?

It does not cause brain injury or developmental delay. Developmental or movement difficulties can coexist and deserve separate assessment. Craniosynostosis is different and may need specialist treatment.

How much tummy time is needed?

Start with short supervised awake sessions and increase as comfortable. AAP September 2026 advice suggests three to five minutes two or three times daily, working toward 15 to 30 minutes total daily by seven weeks. Ask for a personal plan if premature, unwell or struggling.

Should I turn the baby onto their side to sleep?

No. Place them on their back for every sleep. Encourage varied comfortable head turning during awake care and by changing room orientation without pillows or fixing the head in place.

Does every baby need a helmet?

No. A specialist may consider it for selected persistent moderate-to-severe cases. Evidence and local recommendations differ; timing, duration, costs and expected benefit need individual discussion.

Can I do neck stretches myself?

Only use an exercise plan demonstrated for your baby by an appropriate clinician or paediatric physiotherapist. Do not force movement or copy another child’s exercises.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
